lesson.menu_title: The AI Boom in Data Centers
lesson.menu_desc: Reading about how artificial intelligence has changed the data center market, and describing trends and changes to a partner -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- The AI Boom in Data Centers
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Luciana Galleote Cartocci | Lesson 6 -- The AI Boom in Data Centers
lesson.grammar_point: present perfect (for, since, over the last, already, so far) to describe trends and changes in a market

listenings.text: Ten years ago, Latin America was a small data center market. Most large companies kept their data in the United States, and local projects were small. That has changed completely. Over the last five years, demand has grown very fast, and many global companies have built new data centers in Brazil, Mexico and Chile. Brazil has become the biggest market in the region. And since artificial intelligence arrived, the question has changed again. It is not about space anymore. It is about power. The biggest problem for new projects now is finding enough electricity for the new AI rooms, and engineers who know how to cool them.

In Germany, hospital requests have changed a lot. Five years ago, hospitals asked us for more space for servers and a good backup. That was all. Now they have started to use artificial intelligence, for images, for beds, for video. So they have started to ask for something different: rooms for AI servers, with much more power and much more cooling. This year, almost half of our hospital clients have asked us about AI. And they have not changed their first rule: uptime. A hospital cannot stop. So redundancy is still in every project, even the small ones.

I have managed data centers for eighteen years, and I have never seen a change like this. In the past, we cooled everything with air. Big fans, cold air under the floor, and it worked. The new AI racks have changed that. They produce so much heat that air is not enough. So this year my team has installed liquid cooling in two rooms. It means water pipes very close to the servers, which made everybody nervous at first. So far it has worked very well. But I have also learned a lesson: there is a shortage of people who know how to do this, so we have trained our own team.

paras: For many years, a data center was a quiet business. Companies needed more space every year, but the growth was slow and easy to plan. That has changed. Over the last few years, artificial intelligence has created a new kind of demand, and in many countries the market has grown faster than anyone expected.

The reason is simple: AI needs special servers, and these servers use much more electricity. A traditional rack uses a few kilowatts; some new AI racks use five to ten times more. So power consumption has become the first question in every new project, and cooling has become the second. Many old data centers have already reached their capacity, not because of space, but because of power and heat.

Hospitals are part of this story. They have started to use AI to read images, to organize beds and to analyze video in real time. For them, uptime and low latency are not a luxury: they are a question of safety. At the same time, there is a shortage of engineers who know how to build these new rooms. For infrastructure companies that understand both hospitals and data centers, it is a very good moment.
